title: Robots Terminating Neighbours
statement:
There are `n` robots standing in a single row, and robot `i` has an integer value `A[i]`. In one step, a robot may terminate the closest robot to its left or the closest robot to its right (an adjacent robot in the current row). When a robot with value `x` terminates a robot with value `y`, the terminated robot vanishes and the value of the surviving robot becomes `x - y`. The remaining robots close the gap, so neighbours are always taken in the current row.

The robots keep terminating each other until exactly one robot is left. Find the **maximum possible value** of the last robot. If there is only one robot, no step is made and the answer is its own value.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers `A[0], A[1], ..., A[n - 1]`.
outputFormat: Print one integer: the maximum possible value of the last remaining robot.

examples.explanation: Robot 0 (value 1) terminates robot 1 (value 2) and becomes 1 - 2 = -1, leaving the row [-1, 3]. Then robot 3 terminates the robot with value -1 and becomes 3 - (-1) = 4. No other sequence does better.
Robot 2 (value 2) terminates -4 and becomes 6, giving [5, -3, 6]. Then -3 terminates 6 and becomes -9, giving [5, -9]. Finally 5 terminates -9: 5 - (-9) = 14, which equals 5 + 3 + 2 + 4.

hints: Try small rows by hand. Write the final value as a sum of the original values, each with a plus or a minus sign. Which sign patterns can actually happen?
With two or more robots, the very last step subtracts one value from another, so both signs always appear. It turns out any pattern containing at least one plus and at least one minus is reachable.

Ideally every value contributes its absolute value. When that pattern needs both signs but all values are strictly positive (or all strictly negative), one value has to give up its contribution twice over: pick the one with the smallest absolute value.
